newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - April 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - April 22.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Tuesday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* As part of tobacco settlement talks, the tobacco industry is working out a provision which could have cigarette makers raise prices in tandem to fund a $300 billion payment.
* AT&T posted about a 25 percent decline in quarterly profits from continuing operations.
* Fidelity Investments named Gary Burkhead to a new position and appointed Robert Pozen to replace him as the firm's top investment executive.
* ITT Industries agreed to buy Goulds Pumps for $815 million plus $119 million in assumed debt.
* The U.S. budget deficit narrowed 13 percent to $111.28 billion for the six months ended March 31 versus a year-earlier, the Treasury said.
* The U.S. Supreme Court agreed to decide if former employees were banned from certain age-discrimination suits if they did not return severance benefits.
* Fannie Mae is mulling a plan to give homeowners insurance that would pay off their mortgages if they became disabled or died.
* Cordiant said it would split, with advertising agencies Saatchi & Saatchi and Bates becoming separately-traded independent companies.
* Municipal bond invesetors and issuers are voicing concerns about a proposed $7 billion muni bond offering to assist with New York state's takeover of Long Island Lighting.
* The Dow Jonews industrials declined 43.34 to 6,660.21 and the Nasdaq composite fell 18.62 to 1,203.95.
* Saks is said to be getting set to bid $290 million for Barney's, including cash, stock and other payments.
* Short interest on the new York Stock Exchange rose 1.7 percent to a record 3.15 billion shares in the latest month.
* Tele-Communications Inc agreed to buy Kearns-Tribune for $627 million in stock. Kearns-Tribune publishes the Salt Lake Tribune and four other newspapers.
* Technology shares became volatile when Intel moved to lower prices on computer-netowrk hardware.

* Heard on the Street: First it was Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan who rattled the stock market in December then it was renowned investor Warrent Buffett, with a warning the stock market could be overvalued. That's why investors were ready to run for the exits when another market veteran Sir John Templeton, retired chairman of Franklin Templeton Group, uttered the words "bear market."

* Credit markets: Municipal bond investors have taken their lumps in recent years, and they should start preparing for another tough fight. A controversial new municipal bond issuer wants to flood the market with what some are calling the largest muni deal ever - at leat $7 billion in new debt to complete a New York state takeover of Lilco.
